title: Confidential information and why it must be protected
learn: Organisations hold confidential information. Human resources: salaries and benefits, staff personal details. Commercially sensitive: client details, stakeholder details, intellectual property, sales numbers, contracts. Access information: usernames, passwords, MFA details, PINs, access codes, passphrases, biometric data. Reasons: salaries kept private so competitors cannot offer higher wages and staff do not compare pay; staff details to protect privacy and stop competitors contacting them; intellectual property so competitors cannot copy designs; client details so competitors cannot contact clients and to protect client privacy; sales numbers; access information to prevent unauthorised access. Impacts of failing: non-compliance with regulations (fines, loss of licence to practise), loss of trust, damage to image, financial loss (fines, refunds, loss of earnings, terminated contracts), legal action, reduced security.
example: A leaked client list lets a competitor approach the clients, the regulator fines the firm for a data protection breach, and clients stop trusting it.
activity: A dental practice holds staff salaries, patient records, supplier contracts and staff door codes. For each, say which category it belongs to, why it must stay confidential, and one impact on the practice if it leaked.
check: Why is access information described as the key to all other confidential information?

title: Malware, botnets and denial of service
learn: Malware is malicious software. Virus: attaches to files, spreads when run and shared. Worm: spreads by itself across networks through unpatched weaknesses. Keylogger: records keystrokes to steal passwords. Ransomware: encrypts files and demands payment. Spyware: secretly monitors and sends data. Remote access trojan (RAT): disguised as useful software, gives hidden remote control. A botnet is a network of infected devices controlled by an attacker through a command and control server, used for DDoS, spam and password cracking. DoS floods a server from one source; DDoS uses many devices so it is hard to block. Prevention: anti-malware, patching, firewalls, trusted sources, changing default IoT passwords, staff training. Mitigation: offline/offsite backups (ransomware), DDoS protection services, extra cloud capacity, traffic filtering.
example: A ransomware attack is mitigated because the company restores clean files from an offline backup instead of paying.
activity: For a school, choose three types of malware. For each, describe how it could get in, its impact on the school, one way to prevent it and one way to reduce the damage if it happens.
check: What is the difference between a virus and a worm?

title: Malicious hacking
learn: Malicious hackers include hacktivists (political causes), nation states (spying, disruption), organised crime (money) and individuals (curiosity, revenge, money). Password cracking and brute force try many or all combinations; dictionary attacks try common and leaked passwords. Longer passwords massively increase the combinations. Prevention: long passphrases, account lockout, MFA, salted password hashes. Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects a script into a web page viewed by others, which runs in their browsers and can steal session cookies; prevent with input validation and output encoding. SQL injection enters SQL code into an input so it becomes part of a database query; prevent with parameterised queries, input validation and least-privilege database accounts. Buffer overflow writes more data than a memory buffer holds, overwriting nearby memory to crash a program or run code; prevent with bounds checking, safe functions and patches.
example: Typing ' OR '1'='1 into a login box can make a badly written query return every user, because the condition is always true.
activity: A small online shop has a login page, a product search box and a comments section. Identify which hacking attack each feature could be vulnerable to, explain how the attack would work, and recommend a prevention for each.
check: Why does account lockout defeat online brute-force attacks?

title: Social engineering
learn: Social engineering manipulates people using trust, fear, curiosity and urgency. Phishing: mass emails pretending to be trusted organisations, linking to fake login pages. Spear phishing: targeted using personal details. Smishing: by SMS. Vishing: by phone. Pharming: redirects a correct web address to a fake site through malware or DNS changes. Watering hole: infects a website the targets often visit. USB baiting: leaving infected USB sticks to be plugged in. Red flags: look-alike sender, urgency and threats, generic greeting, hidden link addresses, unexpected attachments. Prevention: staff training, email filtering, MFA, verifying requests by another channel, never plugging in unknown devices, disabling auto-run, checking HTTPS and addresses.
example: A finance assistant phones the director on a known number before paying a new supplier, and uncovers a spear-phishing fraud.
activity: Write a short guide for new staff at a bank: describe four social engineering attacks they might face (at least one by phone or text), how to recognise each, and what to do.
check: How does pharming differ from phishing?

title: DNS attacks, insecure APIs, man-in-the-middle and open Wi-Fi
learn: DNS attacks and redirection change DNS records or poison a DNS cache so a real name points to a fake IP address; users land on fake sites. Prevention: DNSSEC, patching DNS servers, MFA on domain registrar accounts, certificate checks. Insecure APIs have weak authentication, missing access control, no rate limiting or return too much data, letting attackers read or change data directly. Prevention: authentication tokens, authorisation checks, rate limiting, input validation, API testing and certification. Man-in-the-middle attacks intercept and possibly alter traffic between two parties. Prevention: HTTPS/TLS, VPNs, certificate warnings, MFA. Open or unsecured Wi-Fi has no encryption or is a fake hotspot. Prevention: VPN, HTTPS only, WPA2/WPA3 on your own networks, disable auto-connect.
example: On café Wi-Fi a VPN encrypts all traffic, so an attacker on the same network sees only scrambled data.
activity: Staff at a sales company often work from hotels and trains. Explain two network threats they face on public Wi-Fi, the impact on the company, and two controls the company should require.
check: Why does HTTPS help protect against man-in-the-middle attacks?

title: Technical vulnerabilities
learn: A threat is something that could cause harm; a vulnerability is a weakness it can exploit. Inadequate security processes: weak encryption (old algorithms, short keys), inadequate password policy (short, reused, default passwords), failure to use multi-factor authentication. Out-of-date components: hardware that is unsupported or cannot run current security software; software with no support or patches, legacy systems kept for compatibility, zero-day bugs exploited before a patch exists; firmware in routers, cameras and printers with known weaknesses and default logins. The window of risk lasts from discovery until the patch is installed. Mitigation: patch management, replacing end-of-life systems, isolating legacy systems, strong policies and MFA.
example: An IP camera with a default password and old firmware is found by attackers scanning the internet and used as a way into the office network.
activity: An accounts firm runs an old unsupported operating system because its accounting software needs it. Explain the vulnerabilities this creates and recommend how the firm can reduce the risk until it can replace the system.

title: Human threats
learn: Human error, e.g. sending data to the wrong person or deleting files: prevent with file properties (read-only, permissions), confirmation boxes and staff training. Malicious employee: prevent damage with immediate removal from premises and immediately suspending user accounts, plus least privilege and audit logs. Disguised criminal: accompany all visitors and check identification. Poor cyber hygiene: lock all unattended machines, do not write passwords down, good password management (password managers, unique passphrases).
example: A receptionist who leaves a PC unlocked lets a visitor photograph customer details; a lock-screen habit prevents it.
activity: A college is dismissing an IT technician. List the steps the college should take, in order, on the day of dismissal, and explain why each step matters.
check: Give two good cyber hygiene habits.

title: Physical vulnerabilities and the impact of threats
learn: Physical vulnerabilities: lack of access control (use entry control systems); poor access control (no tailgating, complex access codes changed regularly, monitor access areas, audit staff access to secure areas); nature of location (protect against shoulder surfing, the environment such as flood, heat and dust, and vandalism); poor system robustness (use rugged machines); natural disasters (offsite backups, disaster recovery sites). Use layers: outer perimeter, building, secure area. Impacts of threats and vulnerabilities: loss or leaking of sensitive data, unauthorised access to digital systems, data corruption, disruption of service, unauthorised access to restricted physical areas.
example: A tailgater follows staff into an office and plugs a device into a network port: unauthorised access to both a restricted area and digital systems.
activity: For a warehouse with a customer entrance, staff door and loading bays, identify one physical vulnerability at the outer perimeter, the building entrance and the server room, and recommend a control for each.
check: What is tailgating and how can it be prevented?

title: Technical defences: settings, anti-malware, detection, hardening and updates
learn: Security settings on hardware and software (BIOS/UEFI passwords, disabling unused ports, secure OS and browser settings): cheap but need knowledge. Anti-malware: function is scanning files, emails and downloads using signatures and behaviour; actions are quarantine, delete, alert; must be updated and may miss new malware. Intrusion detection: monitors network or host activity for suspicious patterns and alerts (IPS also blocks); can give false alarms and needs someone to respond. Device hardening: remove unneeded software, services, ports, accounts and default passwords to shrink the attack surface. Software updates and patches close known vulnerabilities but can cause compatibility issues. Firmware and driver updates fix low-level weaknesses. Air gaps physically disconnect critical systems: very secure but inconvenient and still vulnerable to USB and insiders.
example: Hardening a new web server: remove unused services, close all ports except 443, rename the admin account and apply all updates.
activity: A small charity has ten laptops and one server. Recommend four technical defences from this lesson, and for each give one benefit and one drawback for the charity.
check: Why does anti-malware software need regular updates?

title: Encryption: hashing, symmetric and asymmetric
learn: Encryption scrambles plaintext into ciphertext using a key, protecting data at rest and in transit. Hashing is one-way: it turns data into a fixed-length fingerprint; used for storing passwords (with a random salt) and checking integrity; cannot be reversed; weak unsalted hashes can be cracked. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt (e.g. AES): fast, good for large data, but the key must be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: encrypt with the receiver's public key, decrypt with their private key (e.g. RSA); no shared secret needed and enables digital signatures, but slower. HTTPS uses asymmetric methods to agree a symmetric session key. Diffie-Hellman lets two parties agree a shared key over a public channel: with P=23, G=9, secrets 4 and 3, they exchange 6 and 16 and both compute 9.
example: A website stores the salted hash of a password and compares hashes at login, so the stored password is never readable.
activity: A doctors' surgery needs to store patient passwords, send test results to a hospital, and encrypt laptops. Choose hashing, symmetric or asymmetric encryption for each and justify your choice.
check: Why is hashing not the same as encryption?

title: People and access: policies, vetting, training, MFA, VPNs and APIs
learn: User access policies set rules for who gets what access, passwords, and creating and removing accounts. Staff vetting checks references, identity and criminal records before employment. Staff training teaches phishing awareness, passwords, locking screens and reporting. Software-based access control sets permissions by user or role. Multi-factor authentication combines at least two different factor types: something you know (password, PIN), have (phone code, smart card, security key), are (fingerprint, face). Password managers generate and store unique strong passwords in an encrypted vault protected by a master password. VPNs encrypt traffic for remote working. Certification of APIs tests APIs against security standards before use. Each has benefits (e.g. MFA makes stolen passwords useless) and drawbacks (e.g. slower login, lost device recovery).
example: A phished password fails to unlock an account because the login also needs a code from the employee's authenticator app.
activity: A recruitment agency's staff reuse weak passwords and work remotely. Recommend three controls from this lesson, explain how each reduces the risk, and give one drawback of each.
check: Why is a password plus a security question not true MFA?

title: Backups, port scanning and penetration testing
learn: Backups: full (everything; simplest restore; most storage), incremental (changes since the last backup; quickest; restore needs full plus every incremental), differential (changes since the last full; restore needs full plus latest differential). Safe storage: offsite or cloud copy, an offline copy safe from ransomware, encrypted, restores tested; the 3-2-1 rule is three copies, two media, one offsite. Port scanning finds open ports and services (e.g. nmap -sn to find hosts, nmap -sV for service versions); defenders use it to find services to close. Penetration testing is an authorised simulated attack: plan and agree scope, reconnaissance, scan, exploit safely, report. Ethical hacking has permission and aims to fix weaknesses; unethical hacking has no permission and is illegal. Benefits: finds real weaknesses first. Drawbacks: cost, snapshot in time, possible disruption, testers must be trusted. Only scan systems you own or are authorised to test.
example: An incremental backup on Wednesday copies only files changed since Tuesday's backup.
activity: Design a backup plan for a small architects' office that works Monday to Friday: choose the backup types and schedule, where copies are stored, and how often restores are tested. Justify each decision.
check: What makes a penetration test legal when a criminal attack is not?

title: Firewalls, network segregation and monitoring
learn: Firewall configuration uses rules checked in order: rules for inbound and outbound traffic, traffic type rules (e.g. allow HTTPS 443, block Telnet 23), application rules (block risky apps), IP address rules (block known bad addresses, allow admin access only from certain IPs). Default deny blocks anything not allowed. Network segregation: virtual (VLANs, subnets), physical (separate cabling and switches), offline network (no internet connection) - contains breaches but adds complexity. A DMZ holds public servers separately from the internal LAN. Network monitoring watches traffic, logs and alerts to spot attacks and faults early. Regular port scanning of your own network finds unexpected open services.
example: A rule allowing inbound 443 only to the web server in the DMZ, and denying all other inbound traffic, keeps the internal LAN unreachable from the internet.
activity: A small hotel has staff PCs, a booking server, guest Wi-Fi and CCTV. Propose how to segregate the network and write three firewall rules, explaining the purpose of each.
check: Why should firewalls also filter outbound traffic?

title: The CIA triad
learn: Confidentiality: data is kept private by controlling who has access (access control, encryption, MFA). Integrity: data has not been tampered with; this can be supported by maintaining confidentiality, as fewer people can change it (hashing, permissions, audit logs, validation). Availability: data is available and useful when needed; it is only useful if integrity is maintained (backups, redundancy, DDoS protection, patching). The elements interrelate and must be balanced: too much restriction harms availability. Incidents map to elements: a leak hits confidentiality, altered records hit integrity, ransomware or DDoS hits availability.
example: Ransomware affects availability because staff cannot open their files, and integrity because the files have been changed.
activity: For each incident, state which CIA elements are affected and why: a stolen unencrypted laptop; a DDoS on a ticket website; a student changing their grades in a database; a flood in a server room.
check: Explain how maintaining confidentiality helps protect integrity.

title: Identification, authentication, authorisation and accountability (IAAA)
learn: Identification recognises the individual: knowledge-based (username), possession-based (ID card, fob), biometric-based (face, fingerprint). Authentication verifies the claimed identity: passwords and passphrases, multi-factor authentication, biometric authentication. Authorisation ensures authenticated users only access permitted resources and actions: role-based access control (permissions by job role) and access control lists. Accountability traces actions to the responsible user: audit logs and user activity monitoring. Benefits and drawbacks: biometrics are hard to fake but cannot be changed if stolen; RBAC is easy to manage but roles must be kept current; logs deter misuse but need storage, review and raise privacy concerns. Shared accounts break accountability.
example: Log in as jsmith (identification), enter a password and app code (authentication), open only HR folders because of the HR role (authorisation), with every file access logged (accountability).
activity: A shop's staff all share one till login and refunds are going missing. Use each stage of the IAAA model to redesign how staff use the till, explaining the benefit of each change.
check: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
